title: Levy changes would mean 'obscene' tax rise
full_text:
Kennards Self Storage says it could be slugged $2.2 million more in tax - a huge 990 per cent increase - under changes to how NSW pays for emergency services that would hit industrial and commercial landowners.
The Minns government wants to shift from the emergency services levy (ESL) - a surcharge on insurance that can contribute to the problem of underinsurance - to a general land tax. NSW is the last mainland state relying on an insurance-based levy, which adds up to 18 per cent for household insurance premiums and up to 34 per cent for businesses.
Under five possible options proposed by NSW Treasury the majority of households will be better off, with an estimated $65 a year saving on average. But households with more expensive unimproved real estate, and industrial and commercial landowners, could be forced to pay more.
Sam Kennard, the chief executive of Kennards Self Storage, told The Australian Financial Review his firm currently paid $221,000 for the ESL on 49 insured properties in NSW.
Under option C, one of five models being studied in a NSW parliamentary inquiry, Kennards would be liable to pay $2.3 million on those properties, he said. The figure rose to $2.4 million if a further three uninsured properties, liable for the new tax, were added.
"A 990 per cent increase in a tax is kind of obscene. It's ridiculous," Kennard said.
NSW's tax would be "significantly higher than in any other state". Kennards Self Storage pays $258,000 in Queensland and $293,000 in Victoria, where the ESL tax on land is calculated by capital-improved value.
Kennard said the big impost would not be "unique to a large portfolio owner like us" because it would hit many businesses that owned their own properties, including pubs and smash repair shops, and those who rent because landowners would pass on the additional cost.
"They'll probably cop it. If you're a landlord renting out to a small business or residential household, there'll be a cost to you, you'll want to get that back from the tenant," Kennard said.
"If it's a user-pay apportionment based on demand, then all people using emergency services should be pitching in." Kennard argued that households' contribution to the tax would be "insignificant" compared with that of businesses. Other insured parties, such as car owners, would not contribute at all.
A broad coalition is pushing for ESL reform, including insurers and brokers, Business NSW, the Strata Community Association NSW, NSW Council of Social Service and the Committee for Sydney. Business NSW would prefer the ESL be scrapped and paid for out of general revenue, a position Kennard said would be a "reasonable outcome".
NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey has not committed to legislate before the March 2027 election, but has sought support from the Coalition for the reform. Shadow treasurer Scott Farlow said the Coalition was concerned that up to 45 per cent of residents currently insured would pay more under the five reform options, rising to 55 per cent in Sydney and 85 per cent of people in apartments.
Farlow said Kennard Storage's estimate that it would be liable for a $2.4 million tax bill was an "extraordinary" example. He called on NSW Treasury to publish a calculator for people to assess if they will pay more, as the previous Coalition government did in 2017,
"It would be worthwhile ... so people can make that assessment themselves, whether residential or businesses like Mr Kennard's or small businesses across NSW to work out whether this in their best interests or not."
A NSW government spokesman said that "the current Emergency Services Levy is unfair, inefficient and unsustainable. The government does not have a preferred model and awaits the findings of this inquiry."
According to analysis commissioned by the Insurance Council of Australia, 2.1 million households would be better off under the changes.
